entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10765"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 52</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.34">Jr 52:1-34</reference>. Written by Some Other than Jeremiah (Probably Ezra) AS AN Historical Supplement to the Previous Prophecies</title> <div sID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.51.64">Jr 51:64</reference>). Jeremiah, having already (thirty-ninth and fortieth chapters) given the history in the proper place, was not likely to repeat it here. Its canonical authority as inspired is shown by its being in the Septuagint version. It contains the capture and burning of Jerusalem, &c., Zedekiah's punishment, and the better treatment of Jehoiachin under Evil-merodach, down to his death. These last events were probably subsequent to Jeremiah's time.<div eID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10765"/><hi type="bold">3. through ... anger of ... Lord ... Zedekiah rebelled--</hi>His "anger" against Jerusalem, determining Him to "cast out" His people "from His presence" heretofore manifested there, led Him to permit Zedekiah to rebel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">2Ki 23:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">27</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.9.12">Ex 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.10.1">10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.18">Ro 9:18</reference>). That rebellion, being in violation of his oath "by God," was sure to bring down God's vengeance (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Eze 17:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.18">16, 18</reference>). <div eID="gen19284" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 52 Jr 52:1-34 . Written by Some Other than Jeremiah (Probably Ezra) AS AN Historical Supplement to the Previous Prophecies (See on Jr 51:64 ). Jeremiah, having already (thirty-ninth and fortieth chapters) given the history in the proper place, was not likely to repeat it here. Its canonical authority as inspired is shown by its being in the Septuagint version. It contains the capture and burning of Jerusalem, &c., Zedekiah's punishment, and the better treatment of Jehoiachin under Evil-merodach, down to his death. These last events were probably subsequent to Jeremiah's time. 3. through ... anger of ... Lord ... Zedekiah rebelled-- His "anger" against Jerusalem, determining Him to "cast out" His people "from His presence" heretofore manifested there, led Him to permit Zedekiah to rebel ( 2Ki 23:26 , 27 ; compare Ex 9:12 ; 10:1 ; Ro 9:18 ). That rebellion, being in violation of his oath "by God," was sure to bring down God's vengeance ( 2Ch 36:13 ; Eze 17:15 , 16, 18 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10770"/><div sID="gen19290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10770"/><hi type="bold">12. tenth day--</hi>But in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.8">2Ki 25:8</reference>, it is said "the seventh day." Nebuzara-dan started from Riblah on the "seventh" day and arrived in Jerusalem on the "tenth" day. Seeming discrepancies, when cleared up, confirm the genuineness of Scripture; for they show there was no collusion between the writers; as in all God's works there is latent harmony under outward varieties. <div eID="gen19290" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10776"/><div sID="gen19297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10776"/><hi type="bold">20. bulls ... under the bases--</hi>But the bulls were not "under the bases," but under the sea (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.25">1Ki 7:25</reference>, 27, 38); the ten bases were not under the sea, but under the ten lavers. In English Version, "bases," therefore, must mean the lower parts of the sea under which the bulls were. Rather, translate, "the bulls were in the place of (that is, 'by way of'; so the Hebrew, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.9">1Sa 14:9</reference>), bases," or supports to the sea [Buxtorf]. So the Septuagint. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.16">2Ki 25:16</reference> omits the "bulls," and has "and the bases"; so Grotius here reads "the bulls (which were) under (the sea) and the bases." <div eID="gen19297" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10777"/><div sID="gen19298" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10777"/><hi type="bold">21. eighteen cubits--</hi>but in <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.15">2Ch 3:15</reference>, it is "thirty-five cubits." The discrepancy is thus removed. Each pillar was eighteen common cubits. The two together, deducting the base, were thirty-five, as stated in <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.15">2Ch 3:15</reference> [Grotius]. Other ways (for example, by reference to the difference between the common and the sacred cubit) are proposed: though we are not able positively to decide now which is the true way, at least those proposed do show that the discrepancies are not irreconcilable. <div eID="gen19298" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10778"/><div sID="gen19299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10778"/><hi type="bold">22. five cubits--</hi>so <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.16">1Ki 7:16</reference>. But <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.17">2Ki 25:17</reference> has "three cubits." There were two parts in the chapiter: the one lower and plain, of two cubits; the other, higher and curiously carved, of three cubits. The former is omitted in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.17">2Ki 25:17</reference>, as belonging to the shaft of the pillar; the latter alone is there mentioned. Here the whole chapiter of five cubits is referred to. <div eID="gen19299" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10779"/><div sID="gen19300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10779"/><hi type="bold">23. on a side--</hi>literally, (on the side) towards the air or wind, that is, the outside of the capitals of the pillars conspicuous to the eye, opposed to the four remaining pomegranates which were not seen from the outside. The pomegranates here are ninety-six; but in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.20">1Ki 7:20</reference> they are two hundred on each chapiter, and four hundred on the two (<reference osisRef="2Chr.4.13">2Ch 4:13</reference>). It seems there were two rows of them, one above the other, and in each row a hundred. They are here said to be ninety-six, but immediately following one hundred, and so in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.20">1Ki 7:20</reference>. Four seem to have been unseen to one looking from one point; and the ninety-six are only those that could be seen [Vatablus]; or, the four omitted here are those separating the four sides, one pomegranate at each point of separation (or at the four corners) between the four sides [Grotius]. <div eID="gen19300" type="x-p"/>

Perhaps two were less illustrious persons and are therefore omitted.<div eID="gen19303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">principal scribe of the host--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.33.18">Is 33:18</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10782"/><div sID="gen19305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10782"/><hi type="bold">28. seventh year--</hi>in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.16">14, 16</reference>, it is said "the eighth year" of Nebuchadnezzar. No doubt it was in part about the end of the seventh year, in part about the beginning of the eighth. Also in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1-2Kgs.24.20">2Ki 24:1-20</reference>, ten thousand (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.14">Jr 52:14</reference>), and seven thousand men of might, and a thousand craftsmen (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jr 52:16</reference>), are said to have been carried away, But here three thousand twenty-three. Probably the latter three thousand twenty-three were of the tribe of Judah, the remaining seven thousand out of the ten thousand were of the other tribes, out of which many Israelites still had been left in the land. The thousand "craftsmen" were exclusive of the ten thousand, as appears, by comparing <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">2Ki 24:14</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.52.16">Jr 52:16</reference>. Probably the three thousand twenty-three of Judah were first removed in the end of "the seventh year"; the seven thousand and a thousand craftsmen in the "eighth year." This was at the first captivity under Jehoiachin. <div eID="gen19305" type="x-p"/>

This was at the first captivity under Jehoiachin.
entries.reader_content_plain: 28. seventh year-- in 2Ki 24:12 , 14, 16 , it is said "the eighth year" of Nebuchadnezzar. No doubt it was in part about the end of the seventh year, in part about the beginning of the eighth. Also in 2Ki 24:1-20 , ten thousand ( Jr 52:14 ), and seven thousand men of might, and a thousand craftsmen ( Jr 52:16 ), are said to have been carried away, But here three thousand twenty-three. Probably the latter three thousand twenty-three were of the tribe of Judah, the remaining seven thousand out of the ten thousand were of the other tribes, out of which many Israelites still had been left in the land. The thousand "craftsmen" were exclusive of the ten thousand, as appears, by comparing 2Ki 24:14 with Jr 52:16 . Probably the three thousand twenty-three of Judah were first removed in the end of "the seventh year"; the seven thousand and a thousand craftsmen in the "eighth year." This was at the first captivity under Jehoiachin.
